content: Individuals with sickle cell disease are at an elevated risk of developing community-acquired pneumonia, an acute infection affecting the lung parenchyma. This condition can be caused by a variety of bacterial pathogens, necessitating antibiotic therapy for resolution. However, there is no universally accepted standard for antibiotic treatment in this population, and therapeutic approaches are likely to differ across countries. Consequently, it is important to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various antibiotic regimens for treating community-acquired pneumonia in individuals with sickle cell disease. This review represents an update of a previously published Cochrane Review. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of different antibiotic treatment strategies, whether monotherapy or combination therapy, for individuals with sickle cell disease who develop community-acquired pneumonia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted. The Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register was searched up to September 1, 2016, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches and manual searches of relevant journals and conference proceedings. Additional searches were performed in LILACS (from 1982 to September 1, 2016), African Index Medicus (from 1982 to October 20, 2016), and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry (up to October 20, 2016). The inclusion criteria focused on identifying published or unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated antibiotic treatment approaches for this condition. However, no eligible RCTs were identified during the search process. As a result, no data could be summarized using standard Cochrane methodologies, as no relevant trials were found. The review was unable to provide evidence regarding the efficacy or safety of antibiotic treatments for community-acquired pneumonia in individuals with sickle cell disease. The authors concluded that there is a critical need for randomized controlled trials to determine the optimal antibiotic treatment for this condition. Future trials should adhere to the CONSORT guidelines to enhance the quality of reporting on both efficacy and adverse outcomes in clinical research. These trials should also consider including key outcomes such as the time to resolution of fever, mortality rates, the occurrence of pain crises or other complications of sickle cell disease following pneumonia, diagnostic accuracy, hospitalization metrics (admission rates and length of stay), rates of respiratory failure, and the proportion of participants requiring blood transfusions. Given the absence of relevant trials up to September 2016, the authors do not plan to update this review until new trials are conducted and published.
